slides.title: Title
slides.notes: Open the lecture by shifting attention from a single objective to a whole family of perturbed objectives. The important question is no longer only where the unperturbed function is minimized; it is how the optimal value changes when the perturbation parameter moves. That value curve is where generalized multipliers live.

slides.title: Motivation
slides.notes: Use this slide to justify the new language. In earlier sections, Lagrange multipliers are attached to a particular list of constraints and perturbations. If two formulations have the same feasible objective but perturb different ingredients, they should not be forced to have the same Lagrangian. Bifunctions record exactly that missing information.

slides.title: Definition
slides.notes: Define the object cleanly before attaching optimization language. A bifunction assigns a whole extended-real function to each perturbation vector. The graph function is the ordinary convex function behind the scenes, so students can use familiar epigraph and domain ideas. The projection picture explains why the perturbation domain is convex.

slides.title: Valued Correspondence
slides.notes: Give students a mental model that is less abstract than the definition. A bifunction can be read as a moving feasible set with a cost written on it. When the cost is just zero inside and infinity outside, the object collapses to a familiar set-valued mapping. This makes the terminology feel like a genuine extension rather than a new formal burden.

slides.title: Ordinary Programs
slides.notes: Connect the new language back to the previous section. In an ordinary convex program, perturbing the right-hand sides creates a family of feasible fibers. The associated bifunction is simply the original objective plus the indicator of that fiber. This construction explains why the generalized language preserves the constraint structure that produces Kuhn-Tucker vectors.

slides.title: Generalized Program
slides.notes: Now name the optimization problem attached to a bifunction. The unperturbed objective is the zero fiber, while all other fibers describe allowed perturbations. Minimizing each fiber produces the perturbation value function. This function is the bridge from programs to subgradient theory, so it deserves to be drawn as its own convex curve.

slides.title: Multiplier Theorem
slides.notes: This is the conceptual center of the section. Once the perturbation function is known to be convex, a Kuhn-Tucker vector is simply a negative subgradient at the origin. The sign is important: the price vector compensates for movement in the perturbation direction, so the supporting affine lower bound uses minus the multiplier.

slides.title: Stability
slides.notes: Summarize the corollaries as stability diagnostics rather than as isolated statements. If the origin has enough room inside the perturbation domain, the convex value function has useful finite one-sided derivatives and supporting hyperplanes. Nonexistence corresponds to a perturbation direction where the optimal value drops with infinite speed, while differentiability leaves only one possible supporting slope.

slides.title: Lagrangian
slides.notes: After the value-function theorem, introduce the Lagrangian as the object that will connect this section to saddle-point and duality theory. The infimum over perturbations folds the chosen perturbation model into a function of multiplier and decision variables. For closed proper bifunctions, saddle points are precisely optimal solutions paired with Kuhn-Tucker vectors.

slides.title: Polyhedral Programs
slides.notes: Frame the polyhedral theorem as the clean finite-dimensional case. When the graph function is polyhedral, minimizing over the decision variable preserves polyhedral convexity of the value function. A finite optimal value then guarantees both primal attainment and multiplier existence, and both certificate sets can be studied as polyhedra.

slides.title: Closure
slides.notes: Close the technical arc by explaining why regularization appears. Some bifunctions are natural but not closed, and saddle-point theory asks for closed proper data. Closing the graph function repairs boundary behavior. Under strong consistency, the origin lies safely in the relative interior, so the value function and multiplier set near zero are unchanged.

slides.title: Learner Lab
slides.notes: End with a workflow that students can execute in the notebook. First decide what perturbations the bifunction allows. Then minimize the fibers to draw the value curve, test convexity, and look for a supporting slope at the origin. Finally, if a Lagrangian is available, test the saddle inequalities rather than relying on a visual minimum alone.

slides.title: Recap
slides.notes: Close by compressing the section into four verbs: organize, trace, price, and certify. Bifunctions organize perturbation data; infimum over the decision variable traces the value function; subgradients of that value function give multiplier prices; and closed proper Lagrangians certify optimal primal-dual pairs through saddle points.
